summary.summary: Derbyshire held borrowing flat at £400.9m in 2025/26 but the mix leans on short money: £124.5m is short-term borrowing from other local authorities (average maturity 0.2 years) and 33% of all debt matures within 12 months, in a market where year-end inter-authority rates spiked to 5-7%. Internal borrowing rose £69m to £302.8m as usable reserves fall — partly because reserves are being used to fund the DSG schools deficit — and the forecast balance sheet assumes an £84m SEN refund from government in 2026-27. Investment income strongly overachieved (£10.9m vs £3.9m budget) and the £11.4m Buxton Crescent Hotel loan was repaid in full when the hotel was sold in December 2025. The £50m nominal strategic pooled funds still carry a stated £4.455m unrealised loss behind the statutory override (extended to April 2029), with a £3.9m reserve held against it; all prudential indicators were complied with.

signals.headline: Usable reserves are being used to fund the DSG deficit, lifting the net borrowing requirement from £286.596m to £356.906m at 31 March 2026; forecast balance sheet resources include an estimated £84.051m SEN refund in 2026-27 and £43.689m in 2027-28 and 2028-29
signals.why: The schools deficit is converting into real borrowing need, and the recovery path leans on government refunds that have not yet been received.

signals.headline: 33% of £400.929m borrowing matures within 12 months at 31 March 2026, including £124.500m of short-term local authority loans at 4.46% (WAM 0.20 years; £117.5m taken and £138.0m repaid in year); the report records year-end short-term LA rates of 5.0-7.0%
signals.why: A third of the debt book rolls over annually in the inter-authority market, whose price spiked at exactly the time of year the council refinances.

news_drafts.headline: Derbyshire schools-funding deficit forecast at £173.845m by March 2027, with £84.051m refund expected
news_drafts.lead:
Derbyshire County Council expects its deficit on the dedicated schools grant (DSG, the government grant that funds schools) to reach £173.845m by 31 March 2027, according to first-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget) taken by Cabinet on 10 September. The figure is the £93.390m carried forward from 2025-26 plus a forecast overspend this year of £80.455m.

Almost all of that overspend is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The council forecasts spending of £206.523m against a budget of £127.479m, a gap of £79.044m. The papers attribute it to continuing demand, limited capacity and more use of higher-cost independent placements. Education, health and care plans rose 7.6% to 9,063. The government's high needs grant rose by £6.670m to £133.576m, but the papers say that includes no allowance for inflation or demand growth. The council's performance report puts the backlog of open assessments at 1,600, with 20% of plans issued within the 20-week statutory timescale in the quarter.

The government has said it will refund 90% of the deficit built up before March 2026, £84.051m, expected this autumn. The council must find the remaining £9.339m. The paper says the 2026-27 deficit is not covered, and that the second phase of proposals for deficits to March 2028 is "still to be confirmed. This is a significant financial risk."

Children's Services separately forecasts a £3.187m overspend. Cabinet is asked to approve £1.015m from a budget risk reserve for a restructure of SEND services into a locality-based model. It would carry an ongoing cost of £2.513m a year from 2027-28.

news_drafts.headline: Derbyshire Council published its 2025-26 draft accounts on 14 August, 45 days after the 30 June statutory deadline
news_drafts.lead: Derbyshire County Council has failed to publish its draft financial accounts by the statutory deadline for the second consecutive year, triggering auditor concern about "potentially significant weakness" in its financial reporting arrangements. The 2025-26 accounts were due on 30 June 2026 but were not published until 14 August; the previous year's accounts were similarly delayed to November 2025. The auditor will now investigate whether the recurring delays were accompanied by material errors, poor working papers, inadequate resources or significant audit adjustments. The missed deadlines come as the council faces multiple unfunded budget pressures: its High Needs school funding deficit is forecast to reach £173.8m by March 2027, with services including children's placements and adult care forecasting combined overspends of over £7m and "Red" rated savings judged unlikely to be delivered.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 General and Earmarked Reserves, 10/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: General reserve forecast to increase to £38.171m, driven by £1.181m year-end outturn forecast
findings.detail: The general reserve balance at 1 April 2026 was £36.990m, with no planned contributions or uses during the year. However, the council forecasts a year-end outturn surplus of £1.181m, which would increase the reserve to £38.171m by 31 March 2027, maintaining it at 4.6% of the Net Budget Requirement of £820.359m.
findings.matters: A lender monitoring the council's financial position wants to know if reserves are being maintained or depleted, and whether the council can absorb shocks. A stable or growing reserve position indicates the council is managing in-year finances within or ahead of plan.

findings.headline: Environment directorate held £0.841m uninvoiced debt at Q1, with 86.2% aged beyond 30 days
findings.detail: Uninvoiced debt breaks down as: 0-30 days £0.364m (43.3%), 31-365 days £0.361m (42.9%), 1-2 years £0.116m (13.8%). Total aged debt profile was £1.348m, with no write-offs recorded in the year to 30.06.2026.
findings.matters: Receivables aged beyond 30 days indicate collection difficulties or debtor solvency issues; material portions beyond one year raise bad debt risk.

findings.headline: Transport Development Management forecasting £0.574m overspend against £0.028m net budget; noted as statutory service
findings.detail: Transport Development Management is forecasting £0.574m full-year expenditure against a net budget of £0.028m, a variance of nearly 2000%. The paper notes this is a statutory service, which constrains management flexibility to reduce spend.
findings.matters: Statutory services cannot be underspent or terminated; overspends on mandatory services indicate demand or cost pressures the council cannot avoid.

findings.headline: Environment portfolio forecasting £0.461m overspend against £72.339m net controllable budget at Q1
findings.detail: Full year forecast expenditure of £72.800m against budget of £72.339m represents 0.64% overspend at quarter one 2026/27 across all Environment services including transport, waste, libraries, planning and countryside.
findings.matters: Q1 overspends set trajectory for full-year outturn; if this rate continues, portfolio overspend could reach £1.8m by year-end.
findings.quote: Forecast Net Expenditure 72.800 Forecast (Under) / Over Spend 0.461

findings.headline: Public Transport Levy charged by combined authority for first time in 2026-27; accrual estimate was £0.498m higher than amount now expected
findings.detail: The East Midlands Combined County Authority charged Derbyshire a Public Transport Levy from February 2026 for the first time. The 2025-26 part-year amount was accrued based on an estimate. The amount now expected to be chargeable for 2026-27 is less than this estimate, creating a favourable variance of £0.498m.
findings.matters: New recurring levy from combined authority represents a permanent cost, but initial forecast was more pessimistic than the actual charge. Finance directors tracking new external charges need to establish the baseline and monitor whether it remains stable.
findings.figures: £0.498m favourable variance on levies and precepts
findings.quote: The Public Transport Levy was chargable to Derbyshire County Council from East Midlands Combined County Authority (EMCCA) for the first time from February 2026. The accrued amount for the 2025-26 part-year was based on an estimate and the amount now expected to be chargeable is less than this, resulting in a favourable variance.
